section.title: The Twelve and the Sermon on the Plain
section.sectionRationale: After two clashes over the Sabbath that harden the opposition, Jesus spends a night in prayer and chooses twelve from His disciples, then comes down to a level place and preaches. Luke's Sermon on the Plain is his counterpart to Matthew's Sermon on the Mount: blessings on the poor and hungry, woes on the comfortable, the command to love enemies, warnings against a judging spirit, and a closing call to build life on obedience to His words. It is one movement that moves from conflict, to the forming of the new community, to its charter.
section.thesis: The Lord of the Sabbath forms a new people around Himself and lays out the upside-down life of His kingdom: God's blessing rests on the poor and hated who belong to Him, His people love even their enemies as sons of the merciful Father, and the one who truly hears Jesus proves it by doing what He says.
section.frameNote: Five movements: two Sabbath controversies that reveal Jesus as Lord of the Sabbath; a night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve with healing of the crowds; the blessings and woes; the command to love enemies and refuse a judging spirit; and the tree known by its fruit with the two foundations.

units.label: The Lord of the Sabbath
units.note: grain on the Sabbath and a withered hand restored

verses.text: One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain, rub them in their hands, and eat them.
But some of the Pharisees asked, “Why are you doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?”
Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry?
He entered the house of God, took the consecrated bread and gave it to his companions, and ate what is lawful only for the priests to eat.”
Then Jesus declared, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
On another Sabbath Jesus entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered.
Looking for a reason to accuse Jesus, the scribes and Pharisees were watching Him closely to see if He would heal on the Sabbath.
But Jesus knew their thoughts and said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand among us.” So he got up and stood there.
Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you, which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?”
And after looking around at all of them, He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and it was restored.
But the scribes and Pharisees were filled with rage and began to discuss with one another what they might do to Jesus.

units.label: The choosing of the Twelve
units.note: a night of prayer, twelve apostles, and healing crowds

verses.text: In those days Jesus went out to the mountain to pray, and He spent the night in prayer to God.
When daylight came, He called His disciples to Him and chose twelve of them, whom He also designated as {{apostolos|apostles}}:
Simon, whom He named Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew;
Matthew and Thomas; James son of Alphaeus and Simon called the Zealot;
Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

Then Jesus came down with them and stood on a level place. A large crowd of His disciples was there, along with a great number of people from all over Judea, Jerusalem, and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon.
They had come to hear Him and to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits were healed.
The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all.

units.label: The blessings and the woes
units.note: God's favor on the poor, His warning to the comfortable

verses.text: Looking up at His disciples, Jesus said: “{{makarios|Blessed}} are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they exclude you and insult you and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven. For their fathers treated the prophets in the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort.
Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.

units.label: Love your enemies
units.note: mercy like the Father, and no judging spirit

verses.text: But to those of you who will listen, I say: {{agapao|Love}} your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.
If someone strikes you on one cheek, turn to him the other also. And if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well.
Give to everyone who asks you, and if anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back.
Do to others as you would have them do to you.
If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same.
And if you lend to those from whom you expect repayment, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, expecting to be repaid in full.

But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return. Then your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.
Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.
Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap. For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.”

units.label: The tree and its fruit, and the two foundations

verses.text: Jesus also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?
A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?

How can you say, ‘Brother, let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while you yourself fail to see the beam in your own eye? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.
No good tree bears bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit.
For each tree is known by its own fruit. Indeed, figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor grapes from brambles.

The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.
Why do you call Me ‘{{kyrios|Lord}}, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?
I will show you what he is like who comes to Me and hears My words and acts on them:

He is like a man building a house, who dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock. When the flood came, the torrent crashed against that house but could not shake it, because it was well built.

But the one who hears My words and does not act on them is like a man who built his house on ground without a foundation. The torrent crashed against that house, and immediately it fell, and great was its destruction!”

apostolos.gloss: One who is sent, an envoy or commissioned messenger who carries the authority of the sender. Jesus prays all night and then names twelve, giving them this title. They are not merely learners but delegates, sent to represent Him, and the number twelve deliberately echoes the twelve tribes: Jesus is founding a renewed Israel around Himself.

makarios.gloss: Blessed, happy, and deeply well off, not because of pleasant circumstances but because of God's favor. Jesus pronounces this blessing on the poor, the hungry, the weeping, and the hated who belong to Him. Their present lack is real, but God's kingdom, fullness, laughter, and reward are certainly theirs, so they are already the truly fortunate ones.

agapao.gloss: To love with a deliberate, self-giving love that wills and does good to another, regardless of merit or return. Jesus commands this love even toward enemies, grounding it in the character of God who is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. It is not warm feeling but active goodness, the mark of those who are sons of the Most High.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master, the one with rightful authority. To call Jesus 'Lord, Lord' is to acknowledge His sovereign claim, yet Jesus warns that the title is empty unless it issues in obedience. The word is also used in the Greek Old Testament for God Himself, so calling Jesus Lord carries the weight of confessing His divine authority over life.

basic.context: Two Sabbath scenes open the chapter. Jesus defends His disciples for picking grain and heals a man's withered hand, declaring Himself Lord of the Sabbath, which enrages His opponents. Then, after a whole night of prayer, He chooses twelve apostles and comes down to a level place, where crowds press to be healed. There He preaches: blessings on the poor and hungry and hated, woes on the rich and comfortable, the command to love enemies and be merciful like the Father, warnings against a judging and hypocritical spirit, and a final picture of two builders. The whole sermon asks whether we will merely call Him Lord or actually do what He says.
basic.hermeneutics: The blessings and woes are not praising poverty in itself or condemning wealth in itself; they announce a great reversal for those who belong to the Son of Man, and a warning to those whose comfort is their whole reward. The commands to turn the cheek and give the tunic are vivid pictures of a heart free from retaliation and grasping, not wooden rules that cancel all justice. The closing parable makes the test plain: real hearing shows itself in obedience.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus names twelve apostoloi, sent ones, forming a new Israel. He calls the poor makarios, truly blessed, because the kingdom is theirs. He commands His people to agapao their enemies, to love them with active goodness like the Father. And He asks why they call Him kyrios, Lord, yet do not do what He says.
basic.typology: Jesus choosing twelve apostles echoes the twelve tribes of Israel, marking Him as the founder of a renewed people of God. The Sermon on the Plain stands in the line of Moses giving the law, but now the greater Teacher speaks His own words with authority, and the house built on the rock recalls the wisdom that builds a life on the fear of the Lord.
basic.christ: Jesus speaks as Lord of the Sabbath and as the one whose words are the rock on which a life either stands or falls. He does not merely relay God's will; He is the authority. He blesses the poor and hated because they are His, and He calls people to love enemies as He Himself will love His enemies from the cross. To build on the rock is to come to Him, hear Him, and obey Him.
basic.god: God is the merciful Father who is kind even to the ungrateful and wicked, and His children are to mirror that mercy. He is the God who reverses fortunes, lifting the poor and warning the self-satisfied. And He is the one whose favor, not human approval, makes a person truly blessed.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 5 to 7 gives the fuller Sermon on the Mount. 1 Samuel 21 records David eating the consecrated bread. James 2 develops mercy and true faith that acts, and James 3 the fruit of the tongue. Leviticus 19:18 commands love of neighbor, which Jesus stretches to the enemy.
basic.oneStory: Jesus gathers a new people and hands them the charter of the kingdom. The story of Scripture has always moved toward a God who blesses the humble and lowly and asks for a love that reflects His own mercy. Here the Savior for the poor and outcast makes that explicit, and calls all who hear to build their lives on Him.

context.literary:
Luke 6 falls into three panels, and each one answers a question the one before it raises. In the first, verses 1 to 11, two Sabbath scenes ask who has authority over the day of rest. In the second, verses 12 to 19, a night of prayer and the naming of twelve ask who will carry that authority forward. In the third, verses 20 to 49, the sermon asks what kind of people this new community must be. The panels are linked by the word 'Lord.' Jesus is 'Lord of the Sabbath' in verse 5, and at the end He asks, 'Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?' in verse 46. The chapter begins by claiming His lordship and ends by testing whether anyone means it.

The two Sabbath stories are a matched pair, one about eating and one about healing, one in a grainfield and one in a synagogue. In both the question is the same, what the day is for, and in both Jesus answers by asking a question of His own, 'Have you not read?' in verse 3, and 'which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?' in verse 9. These are the last two scenes in the block of five controversies that began at Luke 5:17, and the chapter's opening line of conflict ends with the opponents in a fury, verse 11.

The sermon is carefully shaped. It opens with four blessings and four woes, verses 20 to 26, which are set in strict parallel, poor against rich, hungry against full, weeping against laughing, hated against praised. The central section, verses 27 to 38, moves from love of enemies to mercy and then to the measure that is given, and verse 36, 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful,' is the hinge. The third section, verses 39 to 45, concerns sight and fruit, the blind guide, the speck and beam, and the tree known by its fruit. The fourth, verses 46 to 49, closes with two builders. The sermon is bound together by the verbs of hearing and doing: 'to those of you who will listen,' verse 27, and 'hears My words and acts on them,' verse 47.

The setting is different from Matthew's. Jesus goes up the mountain to pray and choose the Twelve, and then comes down to 'a level place,' verse 17, where the crowd is. The shape recalls Moses, who went up to meet God and came down to the people, though Luke never says so.
context.historical:
The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant and the most visible mark of Jewish identity under Roman rule. The commandment forbade work, Exodus 20:8-11, and by Jesus' time teachers had built a body of rules defining what counted as work. The disciples were not stealing, since the law allowed a hungry traveller to pluck heads of grain from a neighbour's field by hand, Deuteronomy 23:25. The complaint is that rubbing the grain in their hands was a form of harvesting and threshing on the Sabbath. Jesus answers from the story of David, who ate the bread of the Presence, 1 Samuel 21:3-6, bread that the law reserved for the priests, Leviticus 24:5-9. His point is that need and the presence of the Lord's anointed can outrank a ritual rule.

The second scene was a test of whether healing on the Sabbath was permitted. Later rabbinic rules, which probably reflect older debate, allowed treatment on the Sabbath only when life was in danger, and a withered hand was not. The watchers in verse 7 knew that, and that is why they were watching. Jesus' act of calling the man to stand in the middle makes the matter public.

Choosing twelve apostles carried a national meaning. Twelve was the number of Jacob's sons and Israel's tribes, and Moses had set up twelve pillars at the foot of Sinai, Exodus 24:4. A teacher who chose twelve was making a claim about the renewal of Israel. The list is a mixed company. Four are fishermen, one is Matthew the tax collector, according to Matthew 10:3, and one is 'Simon called the Zealot,' a name that points to ardent nationalism or zeal for the law. A tax collector and a Zealot might in ordinary life have been enemies. Judas Iscariot is named last as the one 'who became a traitor.'

The crowd at the level place is drawn from Judea and Jerusalem and from 'the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon,' verse 17. The last two were Gentile territory, and Luke is telling the reader that the hearers include people beyond Israel's borders.

The sermon was heard by people who knew poverty. Galilee was a land of small farmers, tenants and day labourers, with debt a constant threat. 'Poor' in verse 20 is a word for the destitute, the beggar, not just the person of limited means. To hear 'yours is the kingdom of God' in that setting was to hear a reversal of every expectation. The commands about cloak and tunic, striking and lending also fit a world of robbery, forced loans and collected debts.
context.canonical:
The Sabbath scenes stand in a long line of Scripture about the day. The Sabbath is rooted in creation and in deliverance, Exodus 20:8-11, and Isaiah promises delight to those who honour it, Isaiah 58:13-14. Jesus' appeal to David and His reading of the day's purpose bring out what the law and prophets had said about mercy. In Matthew's account Jesus adds 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Matthew 12:7, and in Mark He says that 'the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath,' Mark 2:27-28.

The blessings and woes have the form of the wisdom and covenant literature. Psalm 1 opens 'Blessed is the man,' and goes on to set the tree beside the chaff, the way of the righteous beside the way of the wicked, Psalm 1:1-6, and Jeremiah 17:7-8 does the same with a tree by the water. Deuteronomy sets blessings and curses before Israel in the same style, Deuteronomy 28:1-2 and 30:19. The woes belong to the prophets' language, as in 'Woe to you who add house to house,' Isaiah 5:8, and 'Woe to those who call evil good and good evil,' Isaiah 5:20. Luke has already prepared the reversal in Mary's song, where the hungry are filled and the rich sent away empty, Luke 1:52-53, and in the manifesto of Luke 4:18.

The call to love enemies has deep Old Testament roots, from the command to love one's neighbour, Leviticus 19:18, to the duty to feed an enemy, Proverbs 25:21. In the New Testament it is lived out and repeated. Jesus prays at the cross, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34, and Stephen echoes Him, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them,' Acts 7:60. Peter says that Jesus 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23, and Paul teaches 'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good,' Romans 12:21.

The closing parables look both to the prophets and to the rest of the New Testament. The call to hear and do is repeated in Luke 11:28 and in James 2:14-17, and Matthew 7:21-23 gives a parallel to the 'Lord, Lord' line. The foundation image returns in 1 Corinthians 3:10-11, where no one can lay any foundation other than Jesus Christ, and in Ephesians 2:20, where the apostles themselves are part of the building. The twelve foundations of the New Jerusalem bear the names of the twelve apostles, Revelation 21:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that Jesus forms a new community and that this community is defined by Him and by His word. The two Sabbath scenes make the first claim: the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, and He interprets the law's purpose by doing good. The night of prayer and the naming of the Twelve make the second: the new Israel is not self-made but chosen by Jesus after communion with the Father. The sermon makes the third: the community's character is mercy, and its security is obedience.

For readers who were poor, hated or excluded, the blessings were meant as comfort and certainty. God's favour is not measured by present circumstances, and those who are mocked for the name of Jesus stand among the prophets. For readers who were comfortable, the woes were a warning that ease can be a snare and that a good reputation may be a sign of compromise. Luke did not write either half for the other half's sake. Luke's Gospel is concerned about the use of wealth, and these words prepare the later parables of the rich fool and the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 12:16-21 and 16:19-25.

Most of all, he meant the sermon to end in a decision. The question 'Why do you call Me Lord, Lord?' pushes every hearer to ask whether his admiration for Jesus has changed his life. Luke wants disciples whose actions match their confession, and he ends the sermon on two houses to make the choice plain.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some of the chapter describes what happened, and some of it commands. The grainfield, the withered hand and the choosing of the Twelve are narrative. They show who Jesus is and are not instructions to hold a vigil on a mountain or to pluck grain on a particular day. The Twelve were a unique group, appointed to be eyewitnesses and foundation stones, and the church does not appoint a new set. What the narrative does teach is that the Sabbath and every other good institution of God is to be read in the light of Jesus' mercy and authority.

The sermon, by contrast, is addressed to disciples and meant to be lived. The commands to love enemies, to bless those who curse, to give and lend without calculation, to be merciful and not to judge are given as the pattern of life for those who follow Jesus. The vivid examples, the cheek and the cloak, are not meant as legal codes to be applied mechanically. They show a heart that does not retaliate or grasp, and Jesus Himself, when struck, did not turn his other cheek in a literal sense but answered with truth, John 18:22-23. The goal is the spirit behind the picture. The command to give to everyone who asks is likewise a call to open-handed generosity, not a rule that cancels all wisdom about helping people well.

The blessings and woes describe what is true of the kingdom and warn, and they do not say that all poverty is righteous or all wealth sinful. The test of the sermon is in verse 47 and 49: to hear and to act.

debates.question: What does Jesus do with the Sabbath?

views.label: He sets aside the Sabbath law
views.case: Some read the scenes as a break with Sabbath observance. The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath and so can overrule it, and the new covenant brings freedom from the old day. Paul later treats days as matters of conscience, Romans 14:5.

views.label: He restores the Sabbath's true purpose against excessive rules
views.case: Jesus does not break the Sabbath commandment but corrects the interpretations. Deuteronomy 23:25 allows plucking grain, and He asks a question that no one can answer, which is lawful on the Sabbath, doing good or doing evil. In Mark He says the Sabbath was made for man, Mark 2:27. On this reading, Jesus is the faithful interpreter of the law and His opponents are the ones who misuse it.

views.label: He claims authority over the Sabbath as its Lord
views.case: The most striking line is verse 5, 'The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.' The title is a claim to authority, not merely to wise interpretation. The one who gave the Sabbath is present, and His authority explains why He may do on it what He does.

debates.bearing: The second and third views are not rivals. Jesus corrects wrong rules and claims the right to do so as the Lord of the day. How believers keep the Sabbath today is a separate question the passage does not settle, but it plainly tells us that the day was given for life and mercy and that its Lord is Jesus.

debates.question: Is the Sermon on the Plain the same sermon as the Sermon on the Mount?

views.label: Two reports of one sermon
views.case: The two sermons share the opening blessings, love of enemies, the golden rule, the speck and beam, the tree and fruit and the two builders, in nearly the same order, and both are followed by the healing of a centurion's servant, Matthew 8:5-13 and Luke 7:1-10. The differences in length and setting would be due to each Gospel writer's selection and arrangement.

views.label: Two different sermons
views.case: Matthew has a mountain and Luke a level place, Matthew nine blessings and Luke four with four woes, and Matthew's sermon is much longer. Jesus taught the same themes many times, and it is natural that He would have repeated them in different settings.

views.label: One teaching, set in different frames by the writers
views.case: Some think that Luke's level place is a stretch of level ground on a mountain, that Matthew and Luke each shaped the material for their own readers, and that the question of whether it was a single occasion matters less than the substance.

debates.bearing: Both accounts give us the words of Jesus, and nothing in the meaning rests on settling the question. What Luke's version makes distinctive is the woes, the stress on the poor and the urgency of mercy, and these are best read as Luke's gift to his own readers.

debates.question: How far does 'turn the other cheek' reach?

views.label: A rule of non-resistance for all situations
views.case: Taken at face value, Jesus forbids retaliation and demands giving to anyone who asks. Some Christians, from the early centuries through the Anabaptists and others, have held that disciples should not use force even in self-defence or on behalf of others.

views.label: A rule for personal wrongs, not for civil justice
views.case: Many hold that the commands concern how a disciple responds when personally wronged, and do not abolish the work of governments and courts, which Paul says bear the sword to punish wrongdoers, Romans 13:4. On this view the church is not told to shut down protection of the weak.

views.label: Vivid pictures that expose the heart
views.case: The examples are hyperbole meant to jolt, as with the beam in the eye. Jesus Himself, when struck before the high priest, questioned the blow, John 18:22-23, which shows that the command is not a literal rule about every blow.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the disciple is not to return evil for evil, to nurse hatred or to grasp his own rights at all costs, and that the pattern is Christ, who 'did not retaliate' and entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The disagreement is over how that applies to defence and justice, and the text itself says more about the heart than about the law.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'poor' in verse 20 is ptochos, which is not the ordinary word for a person of modest means but the word for someone so destitute that he must beg. Luke uses it again of Lazarus at the rich man's gate, Luke 16:20, and in Luke 14:13 Jesus tells His hearers to invite 'the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind.' The first blessing is spoken to people at the very bottom, and the tense is striking. 'Yours is the kingdom' is in the present, while the hungry 'will be filled' and the weeping 'will laugh' are in the future. The kingdom is already theirs, and its consequences are still to arrive.

The woe to the rich in verse 24 says that they 'have already received your comfort.' The verb is apecho, a word used in the language of receipts, 'to have in full.' Matthew uses it in the same sense of those who give to be seen: 'they already have their full reward,' Matthew 6:2. The rich have been paid and the account is closed. The word 'comfort,' paraklesis, is the word Luke uses for 'the consolation of Israel' that Simeon waited for, Luke 2:25. The rich have settled for a small consolation in place of the great one.

'Leap for joy' in verse 23 is skirtao, a verb that Luke uses for the baby who 'leaped' in Elizabeth's womb at Mary's greeting, Luke 1:41. The joy that greets persecution is the joy that leaps at the arrival of the Lord.

The most telling word in the section on love is charis. Three times Jesus asks, 'what credit is that to you?', verses 32 to 34, and the Greek is literally 'what grace is that to you?' Ordinary reciprocity has no charis in it. In verse 35 God 'is kind to the ungrateful and wicked.' 'Kind' is chrestos and 'ungrateful' is acharistos, the one without charis, so the two words play on each other: God is gracious to the graceless. The disciple is to imitate a God whose own favour is given to those who return none. The result is that you will be 'sons of the Most High,' huioi hypsistou, a title Luke has used of Jesus Himself, Luke 1:32.

In verse 36 'merciful' is oiktirmon, the word the Septuagint uses for the LORD's 'compassionate' character in Exodus 34:6. Matthew's parallel says 'perfect,' Matthew 5:48, and Luke's choice of mercy gives a way of reading it: the likeness to God that Jesus asks for is the likeness of compassion. Verse 37 uses a word of release, apolyo, in 'Forgive, and you will be forgiven,' literally 'release, and you will be released,' which brings together the images of captive and debtor that run through this Gospel. The measure of verse 38 is the picture of grain being poured into the fold of a garment, pressed down and shaken until it overflows.

The word 'hypocrite' in verse 42 is the Greek word for a stage actor, a person who speaks behind a mask. The man with a beam in his eye who offers to remove a speck from another's is acting a part. His problem is not simply that he sees poorly but that he plays a role he does not live. The word 'rage' in verse 11 is anoia, which means the absence of understanding, folly or madness. The scribes and Pharisees have watched a man's hand restored and respond with senselessness.

The restoring of the hand in verse 10 uses apokathistemi, to restore to a former state. The same verb is used of the restoration of Israel's kingdom, Acts 1:6, and the hand that is made whole is a small picture of a people being made whole.

The final parable turns on the repeated 'does.' The disciple is the one who 'acts on' Jesus' words, poion, and the tree 'bears,' poiei, its fruit. Luke's version of the builders stresses that the wise man 'dug down deep,' and that the flood is a river in spate, a sight familiar in the wadis of Galilee. The first builder has a foundation and the second 'ground without a foundation.' The difference is not in the hearing, since both hear, but in what they do.

typology.type: The Twelve and the twelve tribes of Israel
typology.fulfillment: Israel began with twelve sons, and at Sinai Moses set up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, Exodus 24:4. Jesus chooses twelve apostles after a night of prayer on a mountain, marking the renewal of God's people around Himself. He says that they will sit on thrones 'judging the twelve tribes of Israel,' Luke 22:30, in 'the renewal of all things,' Matthew 19:28. The pattern finishes in the new Jerusalem, whose twelve gates carry the names of the tribes and whose twelve foundations carry the names of the apostles, Revelation 21:12-14. The type has a limit: the tribes were born into Israel, but the apostles were called from outside, one of them a traitor, and the new Israel is gathered by grace.

typology.type: David and the bread of the Presence, 1 Samuel 21
typology.fulfillment: David, anointed but not yet enthroned, was hungry and received the holy bread meant for the priests, 1 Samuel 21:3-6. Jesus draws the comparison: if the anointed king's need could take priority over the ritual rule, so can the need of the one who is David's greater Son. The bread was set out every Sabbath, Leviticus 24:8, so there is a quiet link between that bread and the Sabbath itself. The escalation is that David was an anointed king in hiding, whereas Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath. The correspondence also reaches its limit, because David took bread for himself and his men, while Jesus will give His own body, Luke 22:19.

typology.type: The tree planted by water, Psalm 1 and Jeremiah 17
typology.fulfillment: The blessed man is like a tree whose roots find water and which yields fruit in season, Psalm 1:3 and Jeremiah 17:7-8. Jesus uses the same figure in Luke 6:43-45 for the one whose heart is good and whose life bears good fruit. The fulfilment comes in Christ and the Spirit. Jesus says 'I am the vine and you are the branches,' John 15:5, and the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace and kindness, Galatians 5:22-23. The tree of Psalm 1 is a picture of a person who keeps the law, and in Christ that picture becomes a gift rather than an achievement. Ezekiel and Jeremiah promised a new heart and a law written within, Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33, and the parable of the tree describes what that heart does.

The Old Testament calls the LORD a rock and speaks of building on a sure foundation. Jesus says that the one who hears His words and acts on them is like the builder on rock, so His words take the place of the LORD's own. In the rest of the New Testament the foundation is Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 3:11, with the apostles as part of the structure, Ephesians 2:19-22. The flood is a picture of judgment, and the secure house is the person who is safe in it. The image stops short of a full picture of grace, since in the parable the builder's work is stressed, and the New Testament adds that the strength to build comes from the Spirit.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first as Lord. At the beginning He says, 'The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath,' and at the end He asks why His hearers call Him Lord and do not do what He says. The title is not a courtesy. It is a claim that He stands where the God who gave the Sabbath stands, and that His words carry the weight of God's. The Sabbath is a day for the people of God to rest in what He has done, and the one who is its Lord is the one who gives rest, Matthew 11:28. When He heals the man's hand He does on the Sabbath exactly what the day was made for.

It leads to Christ as the one who prays and chooses. He spends the night in prayer before He calls the Twelve. The apostles are His gift from the Father's heart, and later He will tell them 'You did not choose Me, but I chose you,' John 15:16. He chooses even Judas, and Luke notes the fact without softening it. He does so knowing the end, and the choice becomes part of the road to the cross.

It leads to Christ as the source of healing and power. 'Power was coming from Him,' verse 19, and the crowd presses to touch Him. The power that restored the withered hand reaches out to all. The Gospel makes it plain that this is a power that gives and does not run out, and it is the same power that will be given to the Twelve to be shared.

It leads to Christ as the one who blesses the poor because He became poor. The One who says 'Blessed are you who are poor' is the one of whom Paul says, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. He does not speak about poverty from a distance. He has no place to lay His head, and He is hated and excluded 'because of the Son of Man,' as He says His followers will be.

It leads to Christ as the one who practises what He teaches. 'Love your enemies' is lived out at the cross: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34. He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked, for He dies for the ungodly, Romans 5:6-8. 'Do not judge' is the way He receives sinners. 'Bless those who curse you' is the way He answers the soldiers who mock Him. Peter says that when He was abused, 'He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. The ethic of the sermon is a portrait of its speaker.

And it leads to Christ as the rock. 'Everyone who comes to Me and hears My words and acts on them' is the one who is safe. The foundation is a person, and the words are His. Paul says that no other foundation can be laid than Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and the sermon tells us what it looks like to build on Him.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The details of the grainfield are not coded pictures of the church's sacraments, the names of the twelve do not carry hidden meaning, and the mountain is not a symbol of Sinai merely because Moses climbed one. The links come from what Luke and the rest of the New Testament say outright: His lordship over the day, His choosing of the Twelve, His poverty and mercy, and His place as the foundation.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the Lord of the Sabbath who made the day for the good of His creatures. The Sabbath commandment grounds the day in God's own rest after creation and His deliverance of Israel, Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:15. When Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good or evil, to save life or destroy it, He is saying what kind of God gave the day. The God of the Sabbath is the God who delights to save, and no reading of His law that prevents mercy has understood Him.

It shows a God who takes the side of the poor and brings about reversal. The blessings are not a general mood but a statement about what God does. Mary had sung that He fills the hungry and sends the rich away empty, Luke 1:53, and here Jesus says that this is how God works. The kingdom is given to those with nothing, and comfort is taken from those who looked for it in what they owned. The God of Scripture has always been the defender of the poor and the one who lifts up those who are bowed down.

It shows the Father whose mercy is the pattern for His children. 'He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked,' verse 35, and He sends the sun and the rain on all, as Matthew has it, Matthew 5:45. This is the heart of the doctrine of God in the sermon. God does not give in proportion to what He receives. He is kind to people who return nothing. Because He is merciful, His people are to be merciful. Holiness in Leviticus 19:2 is shown here as mercy, which does not lower the standard but fills it with content.

It shows a God who judges justly. The woes are not spite. 'Woe' is the prophetic cry of God over those who rely on what cannot save, and the warnings about measure and about fruit show that God sees the heart. The God who blesses the poor also warns the comfortable, and both flow from the same justice and concern. His judgment is also what makes the house on the rock secure, for the flood comes and the house stands.

It shows the God who speaks and is to be obeyed. The final parable makes the point that to hear His word without acting on it is as foolish as building without a foundation. God does not accept a religion of admiration. Throughout the Old Testament He asks for a heart that obeys, and here the same demand is made through His Son, who speaks with the Father's authority. The promise of a new heart in Ezekiel 36:26-27 means that what He commands, He also supplies by His Spirit.

It shows the Father, Son and Spirit at work together in a quiet way. The Son prays to the Father through the night, chooses His apostles and speaks the Father's mercy, and the power that flows from Him is the Spirit's, as Luke has said at Luke 4:18 and Luke 5:17.

For worship, the passage teaches us to come to God without the confidence of the rich and the complacent, to receive His kingdom as a gift and to answer His mercy with mercy. Worship that says 'Lord, Lord' and is not followed by obedience has missed the point. True worship builds a life on His words and is happy to be known as the people whom the Father has blessed.

crossReferences.note: The story Jesus tells to defend His disciples. David, hungry and on the run, receives the consecrated bread from the priest because no other bread is at hand. Jesus uses the story to show that the law's holy things serve human need, and that David's greater Son has even more right than David.

The law that allowed the disciples to pluck grain. A traveller could eat from a neighbour's standing grain by hand but not with a sickle. It shows that the disciples were not stealing and that the objection of the Pharisees was only about the Sabbath, which is why Jesus answers with the Sabbath's purpose.

At the foot of Sinai, Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes and the people accept the covenant. Jesus chooses twelve after praying on a mountain, and the pattern shows that He is constituting a renewed Israel around Himself, with the blood of a new covenant to come, Luke 22:20.

The psalm that begins with 'Blessed' and sets two ways side by side, the tree by the water and the chaff in the wind. Luke's sermon follows the same pattern, from blessings and woes to the tree and its fruit and the two builders. The one who delights in the LORD's word is the one who stands.

Mary's song announces the reversal that the sermon sets out, with the proud scattered, the mighty brought down, the hungry filled and the rich sent away empty. The blessings and woes are the teaching of the same reversal in the mouth of her Son, and show that her song was a prophecy.

The beatitudes in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount. Matthew has nine blessings and speaks of the poor in spirit and those who hunger for righteousness, and Luke has four blessings and four woes in more direct terms. Reading them together helps show both the spiritual and the material sides of what Jesus said.

The command to love one's neighbour as oneself and not to take vengeance or bear a grudge. Jesus stretches the same principle to the enemy, so that the law's call to neighbour love reaches the people who hate you. The command is not new, but its reach is.

Paul applies the sermon in practice: bless those who persecute you, do not repay evil for evil, feed your hungry enemy and overcome evil with good. The passage shows that the early church heard Luke 6:27-36 as a command to be lived, and Paul roots it in leaving vengeance to God.

Peter presents the suffering Christ as an example. He did not retaliate when abused and entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly. It shows that the sermon's ethic of non-retaliation is a description of what Jesus Himself did at His trial and on the cross.

Matthew's version of the conclusion, with the warning about people who say 'Lord, Lord' and the house on the rock. It adds the sad picture of those who prophesied and drove out demons and were still not known. Alongside Luke it makes clear that the test is obedience.

James presses the same point about faith that has no works, which is dead. The two builders of Luke 6 and the sentence 'faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead' say the same thing from two directions. Hearing without doing is the mark of a house without a foundation.

The vision of the bride, the new Jerusalem, with the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and the twelve apostles on its foundations. The choosing of the Twelve on the mountain is the first stone of a structure that is completed in the new creation.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who makes a world and rests on the seventh day, blessing it and setting it apart. The Sabbath is therefore one of the first gifts, a day when human beings are invited to share in God's own rest. Sin spoils that rest, and Israel's story is full of toil and bondage. God redeems His people from Egypt and gives them the Sabbath again as a sign of their freedom. But Israel's history shows how easily a day of rest becomes a burden, and how easily God's people forget why they were given it. In Luke 6 the Lord of the Sabbath comes, and He shows the day's purpose by giving life.

The chapter also answers what the whole Old Testament has been waiting for, which is a people. God had called Abraham to make a nation, and the nation of Israel had its twelve tribes. By the time of Jesus that nation was divided, subject to Rome and often unfaithful. Here Jesus gathers a new core of twelve, drawn from fishermen, a tax collector and a Zealot, and forms them into the nucleus of a people marked by mercy. The blessings give them their identity, the commands their way of life and the parable of the builders their security.

It sets up the chapters that follow. In Luke 7 the Lord who has just taught about faith responds to a centurion and raises a widow's son, and the reversal of the blessings begins to appear. The character of the new community, loving enemies and lending without return, becomes the pattern for Acts, where the church shares its goods and prays for those who kill it. The Twelve are sent in Luke 9, and after Judas falls the number is restored in Acts 1:15-26, so that the apostles can be witnesses to the resurrection.

The cross is the place where the sermon is lived out in full. The enemy is loved, the cheek is turned, the cloak is taken, and the Father is asked to forgive. The Lord of the Sabbath rests in the tomb on the seventh day, and the new creation begins on the first day of the week. The rock on which a life is built is the crucified and risen one.

The new creation is where the blessings are fulfilled and the woes are no more. The poor inherit the kingdom, the hungry are filled and the weeping laugh, for God 'will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4. The twelve names are on the foundations of the city, the Lord of the Sabbath gives an everlasting rest, Hebrews 4:9, and the house built on the rock stands when every flood has passed. The people of God, once a scattering of the poor and hated, are the people in whose midst the Lord dwells.

sermon.title: A Christian Manifesto, Part One
sermon.why: Begg preaches Luke 6:20-27, the heart of the Sermon on the Plain, showing that Jesus' blessings, woes, and command to love enemies expose our need and call for a heart transformed by Christ so that we learn to love what the world hates. A faithful, expository handling of this movement's central section.

quiz.q: What does Jesus claim about Himself in the Sabbath controversies?

options.text: That the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, with authority over it.
options.note: Luke 6:5 records Jesus' direct claim to lordship over the Sabbath.

options.text: That doing good and saving life are always lawful on the Sabbath.
options.note: True and stated in verse 9, but it flows from His deeper claim to be Lord of the Sabbath.

options.text: That the Sabbath no longer matters at all.
options.note: Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; He claims lordship over it and shows its true purpose.

options.text: That the Pharisees were right to accuse His disciples.
options.note: Jesus defends His disciples and exposes the accusers' hardness.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus call the poor and hungry blessed?

options.text: Because the kingdom of God is theirs, and God will fill and comfort those who are His.
options.note: The blessing rests on God's favor and kingdom, promised to the lowly who belong to the Son of Man.

options.text: Because they will one day be rich and full in this life.
options.note: There is real reversal and future fullness, but the promise is the kingdom and reward from God, not simply earthly wealth.

options.text: Because poverty is holy in itself and makes people good.
options.note: Poverty is not saving in itself; the blessing is on the humble who trust God, not on need as a virtue.

options.text: Because God ignores the poor and blesses the strong.
options.note: The opposite is true: God lifts the lowly and warns the self-satisfied.

quiz.q: What does Jesus command toward enemies?

options.text: To love them, do good to them, bless them, and pray for them, as children of the merciful Father.
options.note: Luke 6:27-36 grounds enemy-love in the character of God who is kind to the ungrateful.

options.text: To be polite to them while quietly waiting for revenge.
options.note: Outward restraint is a start, but Jesus commands active love and goodness, not a hidden desire for revenge.

options.text: To love only those who might love you back.
options.note: Jesus says even sinners love those who love them; He calls for more than that.

options.text: To repay evil with evil so justice is done.
options.note: This directly contradicts Jesus' command to love and do good to enemies.

quiz.q: According to the closing parable, what marks the person who truly hears Jesus?

options.text: He comes to Jesus, hears His words, and acts on them, building his life on the rock.
options.note: Luke 6:47-48 defines the wise builder as the one who hears and obeys.

options.text: He calls Jesus 'Lord, Lord' with sincere words.
options.note: Calling Him Lord is right, but Jesus says it is empty unless it issues in doing what He says.

options.text: He admires Jesus' teaching and finds it inspiring.
options.note: Admiration without obedience is exactly the house built without a foundation.

options.text: He hears the words but need not act on them.
options.note: That is the man whose house collapses; hearing without doing ends in ruin.

quiz.q: How does Jesus address a judging, critical spirit?

options.text: By telling us to remove the beam from our own eye before helping with the speck in another's.
options.note: Luke 6:41-42 targets self-righteous hypocrisy while still calling us to help our brother rightly.

options.text: By forbidding every kind of moral discernment about anyone.
options.note: He warns against condemnation, but the same passage tells us to inspect fruit, so it is not a ban on all discernment.

options.text: By saying our faults do not matter as long as we mean well.
options.note: Jesus takes our own faults very seriously; the beam must come out first.

options.text: By encouraging us to expose others' sins freely.
options.note: This is the opposite of His warning against a condemning spirit.

questions: Jesus prayed all night before choosing the Twelve. What would it look like for you to seek God in prayer before your next important decision?

The blessings fall on the poor, hungry, and hated who are Christ's, while the woes warn the comfortable. Where are you tempted to find your security in comfort, wealth, or the approval of others rather than in God?

Jesus commands love even of enemies, grounded in the Father's kindness to the ungrateful. Who is the hardest person for you to love, and what would one act of genuine good toward them look like this week?
Before pointing at the speck in another's eye, Jesus says to remove the beam from your own. Where might you be quicker to criticize others than to face your own faults?
Jesus asks why we call Him 'Lord, Lord' but do not do what He says. Where are you hearing His words without yet acting on them, and what would building on the rock look like there?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts read 'on the second Sabbath after the first' rather than simply 'one Sabbath'; the BSB follows the shorter, better attested reading.
The consecrated bread is literally the Bread of the Presence, set before the LORD in the tabernacle and lawful only for the priests to eat, which sharpens Jesus' point about David.
Luke says plainly 'you who are poor,' where Matthew has 'poor in spirit'; Luke's stress falls on the actual lowly and needy who belong to Jesus, a theme running through his whole Gospel.
